questions.title: Sum of Edge Weights
questions.description:
Weighted graphs are the raw material of every shortest-path and MST algorithm, and the most basic statistic is the total cabling weight on the books. Walk every adjacency list once; each undirected edge is stored in BOTH endpoints' lists, so halve the accumulated sum.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def total_weight(adj):

adj is a weighted UNDIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1; adj[u] holds (neighbor, weight) tuples in input order. Return the sum of all edge weights.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — vertex count and edge count.
Next E lines: u v w — an undirected edge with weight w (stored both ways).

Output Format:
One line with the total weight.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
1 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; 1 <= w <= 100; no self-loops or duplicate edges
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= V <= 50; 1 <= E <= 30; 1 <= w <= 100; no self-loops or duplicate edges

questions.title: Source Vertices
questions.description:
Topological sorting begins at the vertices nobody points at. Count the vertices with in-degree 0 — the natural starting points of a Kahn sweep. Isolated vertices (no edges at all) also have in-degree 0 and count.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def source_count(adj):

adj is a DIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1. Return the number of vertices with no incoming edges.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — vertex count and edge count.
Next E lines: u v — a directed edge u -> v.

Output Format:
One line with the number of in-degree-0 vertices.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; no self-loops or duplicate edges

questions.title: Can Reach the Server
questions.description:
Before scheduling work across a cluster, verify the two endpoints are actually in the same component. One depth-first sweep from the source settles it: if the target turns up among the visited vertices, the answer is yes.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def can_reach(adj, src, dst):

adj is an UNDIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1. Return True when dst is reachable from src, False otherwise. The harness prints True or False.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — vertex count and edge count.
Next E lines: u v — an undirected edge (stored both ways).
Last line: the queried pair src dst.

Output Format:
One line, True or False.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= src, dst < V; no self-loops or duplicate edges
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= V <= 50; 0 <= E <= 30; no self-loops or duplicate edges

questions.description:

questions.title: Fiber Budget Sweep
questions.description:
A fiber crew installs the CHEAPEST cables first — the opening move of Kruskal's algorithm. Given every candidate cable's cost and a budget, sort the costs ascending and lay cables until the money runs out; report how many cables were laid.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def affordable_cables(adj, budget):

adj is a weighted UNDIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1 (each edge stored twice). Collect each edge weight once (use the v > u trick), sort ascending, and greedily take cables while the running total stays within budget. Return the count of affordable cables.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — junction count and cable count.
Next E lines: u v w — a cable with cost w (stored both ways).
Last line: the budget.

Output Format:
One line with the number of cables that fit the budget.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
1 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; 1 <= w <= 100; 1 <= budget <= 10000; no duplicate cables
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= V <= 50; 1 <= E <= 30; 1 <= w <= 100; 1 <= budget <= 10000; no duplicate cables

questions.title: Directed Cycle Sensor
questions.description:
A dependency tracker must reject circular dependencies. The classic detector colors vertices during a depth-first search: 0 = untouched, 1 = on the CURRENT recursion path, 2 = finished. An edge into a vertex flagged 1 is a back edge — proof of a cycle. No imports — pure Python only.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def has_cycle(adj):

adj is a DIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1. Keep a color map (named color) and return True when the graph contains a directed cycle, False otherwise. The harness prints True or False.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — vertex count and edge count.
Next E lines: u v — a directed edge u -> v.

Output Format:
One line, True or False.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; no self-loops or duplicate edges
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= V <= 50; 0 <= E <= 30; no self-loops or duplicate edges

questions.title: Undirected Cycle Sweep
questions.description:
Building a redundant loop into a road network is fine — but planners still want to know when one exists. For an UNDIRECTED graph, a depth-first sweep detects cycles by remembering the parent each vertex was reached from: meeting an already-visited neighbor that is not your parent closes a cycle. No imports — pure Python only.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def has_cycle(adj):

adj is an UNDIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1 (no self-loops, no duplicate edges). Track a visited set and return True when the graph contains a cycle, False otherwise. The harness prints True or False.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — vertex count and edge count.
Next E lines: u v — an undirected edge (stored both ways).

Output Format:
One line, True or False.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; no self-loops or duplicate edges

questions.description:
Every flight leg is a transfer-free hop; passengers care about the FEWEST hops between two airports. A breadth-first sweep expands whole levels and records when each airport is first reached — its level is the hop count. Disconnected pairs report -1. No imports (and no deque) — pure Python only.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — airport count and route count.
Next E lines: u v — a route (stored both ways).
Last line: the queried pair src dst.

Output Format:
One line with the fewest-hops distance, 0, or -1.

1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= src, dst < V; no duplicate routes

questions.title: Same Depot Group
questions.description:
A logistics company keeps depots in merged groups as routes open: union-find (disjoint sets) merges two groups in almost-constant time. Build the groups from every link with union operations, then answer each depot-pair query: are the two depots in the same group? No imports — pure Python only.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def connected_answers(V, edges, queries):

V is the depot count, edges a list of (u, v) links and queries a list of (u, v) pairs. Maintain a parent list (named parent) with a find helper, union the endpoints of every edge, then answer each query by comparing roots. Return the list of booleans in query order; the harness prints one True/False per line.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — depot count and link count.
Next E lines: u v — a link.
Next line: Q — the query count.
Next Q lines: u v — a queried pair.

Output Format:
One line per query, True or False.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
1 <= Q <= 20
0 <= u, v < V

questions.title: Kruskal Cable Total
questions.description:
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm sorts every edge by weight and sweeps: accept an edge when it joins two different components (checked with union-find), skip it when it would close a cycle. Sum the accepted weights — that is the cheapest total cabling that keeps all depots connected. No imports or heapq — pure Python only.

The program scaffolding (input reading and edge-list building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def mst_weight(V, edges):

V is the depot count; edges is a list of (w, u, v) tuples in input order. Sort the list with sorted (tuples compare weight-first), maintain a parent list for union-find, and return the total weight of the spanning tree (the graph is connected).

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — depot count and cable count.
Next E lines: u v w — a cable with weight w.

Output Format:
One line with the minimum spanning tree weight.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
V-1 <= E <= 60
0 <= u, v < V; 1 <= w <= 100; the graph is connected; no duplicate cables
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= V <= 50; V-1 <= E <= 60; 1 <= w <= 100; connected; no duplicate cables

questions.title: Build Order Smallest First
questions.description:
A build server must schedule tasks with dependencies. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly takes any task whose in-degree dropped to 0 — and the pipeline policy breaks ties by the SMALLEST task index to keep builds reproducible. Output the full order. The graph is guaranteed acyclic; no imports or heapq — scan for the smallest ready index each round.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def topo_order(adj):

adj is the dependency adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1 (edge u -> v means u before v). Track an indeg map, repeatedly pick the smallest-index vertex with indeg 0, append it to the order and decrement its targets' in-degrees. Return the topological order list; the harness prints it space-separated.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — task count and dependency count.
Next E lines: u v — task u must run before task v.

Output Format:
One line with V task indices in Kahn order (smallest index tie-break), space-separated.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; the graph is a DAG; no self-loops or duplicate edges
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= V <= 50; 0 <= E <= 30; the graph is a DAG; no self-loops or duplicate edges

questions.title: Fastest Delivery Route
questions.description:
A courier map is one-way streets with travel minutes. Dijkstra's algorithm grows a settled set: each round pick the UNSETTLED vertex with the smallest tentative distance, relax its outgoing edges, repeat. Report the fastest time from depot 0 to hub n-1 — or -1 when the hub is unreachable. No imports or heapq — a linear scan for the minimum works fine at this scale.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def shortest_distance(adj):

adj is a weighted DIRECTED adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1 (adj[u] holds (v, w) tuples); the source is 0 and the target is len(adj) - 1. Keep a dist map, sweep with the settled-set loop, and return the shortest distance to the last vertex or -1.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — intersection count and street count.
Next E lines: u v w — a one-way street from u to v taking w minutes.

Output Format:
One line with the fastest 0 -> n-1 travel time, or -1.

Constraints:
2 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 60
0 <= u, v < V; 1 <= w <= 100; no self-loops or duplicate streets

questions.title: Two-Team Assignment
questions.description:
A club splits members into two rival-free teams: every grudge edge must cross between the teams. This is exactly bipartiteness — try to 2-color the graph with colors 0/1 so that no edge joins equal colors; an odd cycle makes it impossible. No imports — pure Python only.

The program scaffolding (input reading and adjacency building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def is_bipartite(adj):

adj is the grudge adjacency dict keyed 0..V-1 (undirected, may be disconnected). Keep a color map (named color): color each unvisited component start 0, propagate the opposite color along edges, and return False the moment an edge joins equal colors — True if the whole graph colors cleanly. The harness prints True or False.

Input Format:
Line 1: V E — member count and grudge count.
Next E lines: u v — a grudge (stored both ways).

Output Format:
One line, True or False.

Constraints:
1 <= V <= 50
0 <= E <= 30
0 <= u, v < V; no self-loops or duplicate grudges

questions.title: Counting the Islands
questions.description:
A warehouse floor map is a grid of characters: '1' cells are occupied racks, '0' cells are free floor. Two occupied cells belong to the same island when they touch horizontally or vertically (NOT diagonally). Flood-fill each unvisited occupied cell to count the islands. No imports — pure Python only.

The program scaffolding (input reading and grid building) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def count_islands(grid, R, C):

grid is a list of R strings of length C ('0'/'1' characters). Keep a seen matrix (named seen), flood-fill with a stack over the four directions, and return the number of islands.

Input Format:
Line 1: R C — grid height and width.
Next R lines: C characters each ('0' or '1').

Output Format:
One line with the number of islands.

Constraints:
1 <= R, C <= 10
grid characters are '0' or '1'
